title: Hands-on Coding Questions
intro: Senior Node.js interviews almost always include a "write it from scratch" round: Promise.all, a concurrency pool, an EventEmitter, debounce, an LRU cache, a rate limiter. Interviewers are not testing memory of library code; they watch how you handle ordering, errors, edge cases, timers and memory. A senior answer states the approach first, writes clean code that handles the empty and failure cases, gives the complexity, and names the production trade-offs (cancellation, per-process state, unbounded growth).

questions.title: Implement Promise.all
questions.question: Write your own version of Promise.all from scratch. Then tell me how Promise.allSettled is different.
questions.short: I return a new promise, wrap every input with Promise.resolve so plain values work, and store each result at its own index so the output order matches the input order, not the finish order. I count how many have fulfilled and resolve when the count equals the length. The first rejection rejects the whole thing right away. An empty input resolves to an empty array. allSettled never rejects: it waits for every input and gives back objects like { status, value } or { status, reason }.
questions.simple: It is like waiting for a group of friends to arrive before dinner: you write each name in a fixed seat, start eating when every seat is full, and cancel dinner the moment anyone says they cannot come.

explain.p: Write `promiseAll(iterable)` that behaves like `Promise.all`: it takes an iterable of promises or plain values and returns one promise. That promise fulfills with an array of results in input order, or rejects with the first rejection reason.

list: Turn the iterable into an array first (it may be a Set or a generator, and you need its length).
Wrap every item with `Promise.resolve(item)` so plain values and thenables work the same as real promises.
Store each value at `results[i]`, using the index captured by the closure, so order matches the input.
Count fulfilled items with a counter. Do not use `results.length`: assigning `results[5]` first already makes the length 6.
Pass `reject` straight in as the rejection handler. A promise can only settle once, so later calls to `resolve` or `reject` are ignored.
Handle the empty input: resolve with `[]` immediately, or the promise would hang forever.
Time: O(n) to attach handlers; total wait time is the slowest input (or the first rejection).
Space: O(n) for the results array.
Empty input resolves to `[]` right away instead of hanging.
Plain values and thenables are allowed because of `Promise.resolve`.
Rejection does not cancel the other operations. They keep running; their results are just ignored. Cancellation needs an `AbortSignal`.
Holes: if you used `results.push` you would get finish order, which is wrong.

explain.note: What interviewers look for: the index-based write (order preserved), a counter instead of `results.length`, the empty-array case, `Promise.resolve` wrapping for non-promise values, and knowing that rejection does not stop the other work.

anim.title: Tracing promiseAll with timers and one rejection

steps.note: Calling wait() starts the timers before promiseAll even runs. Promises represent work that is already happening.
Each item is wrapped with Promise.resolve, so the plain string 'c' becomes an already-fulfilled promise. Its .then callback goes to the microtask queue.
The second call starts a 200ms timer and gets an already-rejected promise. We now have two independent promiseAll calls in flight.
The script finishes, microtasks run. 'c' is stored at index 2, not at the front, because we write by index.
The rejected input calls reject on the second outer promise. It fails immediately; it does not wait for x.
At 100ms b arrives and lands at index 1. The counter is 2 of 3, so we keep waiting.
At 200ms x still settles. Rejection did not cancel it: x is stored in the second call's own results, but that outer promise already rejected, so its result is simply ignored.
At 300ms a arrives at index 0. The counter reaches 3, which equals the length, so we resolve.
The final array is in input order even though the finish order was c, b, a.

followups.q: How would you implement Promise.race?
followups.a: Return a new promise and call `Promise.resolve(item).then(resolve, reject)` for every item. Whichever settles first wins because a promise can only settle once. Note that `race([])` stays pending forever.

followups.q: How is Promise.any different?
followups.a: `any` fulfills with the first fulfilled value and ignores rejections. It only rejects when every input rejects, and then it rejects with an `AggregateError` holding all the reasons.

followups.q: If one promise rejects, do the others stop?
followups.a: No. Promises are not cancellable. The other operations keep running and use resources. To stop them, pass an `AbortSignal` into each task and abort it in the catch.

mistakes: Using `results.push(value)`, which records finish order instead of input order.
Checking `results.length === n` instead of a counter; sparse assignment makes length wrong.
Forgetting the empty-array case, so the promise never resolves.
Calling `.then` directly on items, which crashes on plain values like numbers.

questions.title: Concurrency-limited promise pool
questions.question: You have 10,000 URLs to fetch, but you must never have more than 5 requests in flight. Write a function that runs async tasks with a concurrency limit and returns the results in order.
questions.short: I start `limit` workers. Each worker loops: it takes the next index from a shared counter, awaits that task, stores the result at that index, and takes another. Because JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time, `next++` is safe without locks. I wait for all workers with Promise.all and return the results array. Tasks are functions, not promises, so they only start when a worker picks them up.
questions.simple: Think of a bank with 5 tellers and a line of customers. A teller finishes one customer and calls the next one in line. There are never more than 5 people being served.

explain.p: Write `runWithLimit(tasks, limit)` where `tasks` is an array of functions that return promises. Run at most `limit` at once. Resolve with all results in input order. Reject on the first error (or collect errors, if asked).

list: Tasks must be functions (`() => fetch(url)`), not promises. A promise has already started; you cannot limit work that is already running.
Keep a shared `next` index. Start `min(limit, tasks.length)` worker loops.
Each worker: `while (next < tasks.length)` take `i = next++`, `await tasks[i]()`, store `results[i]`.
There is no race on `next++`: the check and the increment run synchronously, and nothing else can run between them.
When a worker finds the queue empty it returns. `Promise.all(workers)` resolves when the last one finishes.
Time: total wall time is roughly a greedy, in-order packing of tasks into `limit` lanes (not the optimal packing). Overhead is O(n).
Space: O(n) for results plus O(limit) live promises, instead of n promises at once.
Empty task list: zero workers, `Promise.all([])` resolves to an empty result right away.
Error handling: this version rejects on first error but lets in-flight tasks finish. For "collect everything" store `{ status, value | reason }` per index instead of throwing.
For huge inputs (millions of items) take tasks from an iterator instead of an array so you do not build them all up front.

explain.note: Why not chunk into batches of 5 with Promise.all? Batching waits for the slowest task in each batch, so lanes sit idle. A worker pool keeps all 5 slots busy all the time.

What interviewers look for: tasks as functions (lazy start), a pool rather than fixed batches, results kept in order, the reasoning for why `next++` is safe in single-threaded JS, and a clear story for errors. Mentioning `p-limit` as the library you would use in production is a plus.

anim.title: Two workers sharing four tasks

steps.note: limit is 2, so we create 2 workers. Nothing has started yet; tasks are just functions waiting in line.
Worker 1 checks next < 4, takes index 0 and bumps next to 1 in the same synchronous step.
Worker 1 hits await and pauses. That gives worker 2 its turn: it takes index 1. Now 2 tasks run, which is the limit.
At 100ms t1 finishes. Its result goes to index 1.
Worker 2 loops and immediately takes t2. The slot did not sit idle, unlike a batch approach.
At 200ms t2 finishes and worker 2 takes the last task, t3.
At 250ms t3 finishes. The while check fails (next is 4), so worker 2 returns. Only worker 1 is still busy.
At 300ms the slow t0 finishes. Worker 1 finds nothing left and returns too.
Promise.all over the workers resolves. Results are in input order. Total time is about 300ms instead of 550ms one by one.

followups.q: Why not just Promise.all(urls.map(fetch))?
followups.a: That starts every request at once. With 10,000 URLs you exhaust sockets and memory, hit rate limits, and may overload the downstream service. The pool caps the work in flight.

followups.q: How would you make it stream results instead of returning an array?
followups.a: Make it an async generator, or accept an `onResult(i, value)` callback. For ordered streaming you buffer finished results and yield them when the next expected index is ready.

followups.q: How would you add a timeout per task?
followups.a: Wrap each task call with a `withTimeout` helper that races the task against a timer and aborts an `AbortController` passed into the task, so the slot is freed and the work is cancelled.

mistakes: Passing promises instead of functions, so all work has already started and the limit does nothing.
Using fixed batches with Promise.all, which leaves slots idle waiting for the slowest item.
Pushing results as they finish, which loses input order.
Adding a mutex around `next++`; it is not needed in single-threaded JS and shows a gap in understanding.

questions.title: Implement an EventEmitter
questions.question: Implement a small EventEmitter class with on, once, off and emit.
questions.short: I keep a Map from event name to an array of listeners. `on` pushes, `off` removes one matching listener, `emit` calls listeners synchronously in the order they were added and returns whether there were any. `once` registers a wrapper that removes itself and then calls the real listener; I store the original on the wrapper so `off(name, original)` still works. In emit I loop over a copy of the array so listeners that remove themselves do not make me skip the next one.
questions.simple: It is a notice board: people sign up for a topic, and when news on that topic arrives you call everyone on the list, in sign-up order, right away.

explain.p: Build `Emitter` with `on(name, fn)`, `once(name, fn)`, `off(name, fn)` and `emit(name, ...args)`. It should behave like Node's `EventEmitter` for these basics: synchronous calls, registration order, chaining (`on` returns `this`), and `emit` returning `true` if anyone listened.

list: Store listeners in `Map<string, Function[]>`. Arrays keep order and allow the same function twice, like Node.
`once` wraps the listener. The wrapper calls `off` on itself first, then calls the original. Removing first means a listener that emits the same event again does not loop forever.
Save `wrapper.original = fn` so `off(name, fn)` can find and remove a pending once-listener.
`emit` iterates over a snapshot (`[...list]`). Without it, `splice` during iteration shifts items and you skip one.
Special case like Node: emitting `"error"` with no listener should throw.
`on`: O(1). `off`: O(k) where k is listeners for that event. `emit`: O(k) plus the copy.
Listeners run synchronously, inside `emit`. A slow listener blocks the emitter and everything after it.
A listener that throws stops the remaining listeners and the error bubbles out of `emit`.
Removing during emit is safe because of the snapshot; a listener added during emit is not called in that same emit (also Node's behavior).
Memory leaks: listeners that are never removed keep their closures alive. Node warns after 10 listeners per event (`setMaxListeners`).

explain.note: What interviewers look for: the snapshot in emit, `once` removing itself before calling, `off` working with once-wrapped listeners, returning `this` for chaining, and knowing emit is synchronous. Bonus: the `"error"` event rule and the max-listeners leak warning.

anim.title: on, once, emit and off on a "join" event

steps.note: on creates the 'join' array in the Map and pushes greet.
once does not store the function directly. It stores a wrapper that knows how to remove itself, with .original pointing to the real function.
emit('join', 'Ann') copies the list first, then calls listeners in order, synchronously. greet runs first.
The wrapper runs. It removes itself from the real list first, then calls the original. The snapshot is untouched, so no listener is skipped.
emit returns true because at least one listener was registered.
Second emit: only greet is left, because the once-listener removed itself.
off finds greet by reference and splices it out. The array is now empty, so the 'join' key is deleted to keep the Map clean.
No listeners for join, so emit returns false. Nothing is called.

followups.q: Are EventEmitter listeners called asynchronously?
followups.a: No. `emit` calls every listener synchronously, in registration order, before it returns. If you want async behavior, the listener itself must defer with `setImmediate` or `queueMicrotask`.

followups.q: What does events.once(emitter, name) do?
followups.a: It is a helper in `node:events` that returns a promise resolving with the event arguments the next time the event fires, and rejecting if `"error"` fires first. It is handy with `await`.

followups.q: What is the MaxListenersExceededWarning?
followups.a: Node prints it when more than 10 listeners (by default) are added for one event. It usually means a leak, such as adding a listener per request and never removing it. You can raise the limit with `setMaxListeners`, but fix the leak first.

mistakes: Iterating over the live array in emit, so a once-listener that removes itself causes the next listener to be skipped.
Making `off` unable to remove a listener registered with `once`.
Calling the once-listener before removing it, which can recurse forever if the listener emits the same event.
Thinking emit is asynchronous or that it awaits async listeners.

questions.title: Implement debounce
questions.question: Implement debounce(fn, wait). Explain where you would use it on the server side.
questions.short: Debounce delays a call until there has been `wait` ms of quiet. Each new call clears the pending timer and starts a new one, so only the last call in a burst runs, with its arguments and its `this`. I keep the timer in a closure and add `cancel` and often `flush`. On the server I use it for things like batching file-watcher events or coalescing config reloads.
questions.simple: It is an elevator door: every time someone walks in, the door timer restarts. The door only closes once nobody has come in for a few seconds.

explain.p: Write `debounce(fn, wait)` that returns a new function. When the new function is called many times in a row, `fn` should run once, `wait` ms after the last call, with the last arguments.

list: Keep `timer` (and the latest args/this) in the closure.
On each call: `clearTimeout(timer)`, then `setTimeout` again. Clearing a null or finished timer is safe.
Use a regular `function` for the returned wrapper so `this` is the caller's `this`, and forward it with `fn.apply(this, args)`.
Add `cancel()` to drop a pending call and `flush()` to run it now. Optionally support `leading: true` to fire on the first call of a burst.
O(1) time and memory per call.
Under a constant stream of calls, a trailing-only debounce never fires (starvation). If you need a guaranteed run, use throttle or a `maxWait` option.
Return value: the debounced function cannot return `fn`'s result synchronously. If callers need it, return a promise that resolves when the call actually runs.
Timers keep the process alive. Call `cancel()` on shutdown, or `timer.unref()` for background work.
Server examples: coalescing `fs.watch` events (one save fires several), reloading config, flushing a write buffer after activity stops.

explain.note: What interviewers look for: clearing and resetting the timer, preserving `this` and the latest arguments, a `cancel` method, and knowing the difference from throttle (debounce waits for quiet; throttle runs at a steady rate).

anim.title: Debounce collapses a typing burst

steps.note: debounce returns a wrapper. The timer variable lives in its closure, shared across all calls.
At t=0 save('h') runs. clearTimeout(null) does nothing, then a timer is set for t=100.
At t=50 save('he') arrives. The 'h' timer is cleared before it fires and a new one is set for t=150.
At t=100 save('hey') resets the timer again, to t=200. The original t=100 timer was already cancelled, so nothing fires here.
There were 100ms with no calls, so the timer fires. Only the last arguments are used. Three calls became one.
At t=400 a new burst starts. A fresh timer is set for t=500.
No more calls arrive, so at t=500 the save runs once with "hey!".

followups.q: What does a "leading" debounce do?
followups.a: It runs `fn` on the first call of a burst and then ignores calls until there has been `wait` ms of quiet. It is useful when you want an instant response, like a button that should not double-submit.

followups.q: How would you make the debounced function return a promise?
followups.a: Keep a list of pending resolvers. Each call creates a promise and stores its resolve/reject. When `fn` finally runs, settle all stored promises with its result, then clear the list.

followups.q: What is maxWait?
followups.a: A cap on how long calls can be delayed. If calls keep coming, `fn` is forced to run once `maxWait` ms have passed since the first call of the burst. With `maxWait === wait` debounce behaves like throttle.

mistakes: Using an arrow function for the returned wrapper and losing the caller's `this`.
Creating the timer variable inside the wrapper instead of the closure, so it is never shared and never cleared.
Confusing debounce with throttle.
Forgetting a way to cancel, leaving timers that keep the process alive on shutdown.

questions.title: Implement throttle
questions.question: Implement throttle(fn, wait) so fn runs at most once every wait ms. Make sure the last call in a burst is not lost.
questions.short: Throttle limits how often fn runs: at most once per window. I track the time of the last run. If the window has passed, I run immediately (leading edge). Otherwise I save the latest arguments and, if no timer exists, schedule one for the remaining time (trailing edge), so the final value is never dropped. Calls inside the window only update the saved arguments.
questions.simple: It is like a bus that leaves every 10 minutes. You can show up any time, but the bus leaves on its schedule and takes whoever is waiting at that moment.

explain.p: Write `throttle(fn, wait)`. During a steady stream of calls, `fn` should run right away on the first call, then at most once per `wait` ms, and one final time with the latest arguments after the stream stops.

list: Remember `last` (when fn last ran), the pending `timer`, and `pendingArgs`.
On each call compute `remaining = wait - (now - last)`.
If `remaining <= 0`: clear any trailing timer, set `last = now`, run fn now.
Else: store the latest args. If there is no trailing timer yet, schedule one for `remaining` ms that runs fn with whatever args are stored then.
Debounce resets its timer on every call; throttle never resets it. That is the key difference.
O(1) per call.
`Date.now()` can jump if the system clock changes. For strict intervals use `performance.now()`, which is monotonic.
Without the trailing timer, the last update in a burst is lost (for example, the final scroll position or the final progress percentage).
Server examples: logging progress at most once per second, sending metrics, limiting how often a cache warm-up runs.
Throttle limits calls inside one process. It is not a rate limiter for clients; for that use a token bucket per key.

head: Debounce
Throttle
rows: at most once per wait ms

explain.note: What interviewers look for: both leading and trailing behavior, using the latest arguments on the trailing call, not resetting the timer, and a crisp explanation of debounce vs throttle.

anim.title: Throttle with leading and trailing calls

steps.note: throttle creates the closure. last is 0, which is far in the past, so the first call will run at once.
At t=0, remaining is negative, so fn runs immediately (leading edge) and last becomes t=0.
At t=50 we are inside the window: remaining is about 150ms. Save the args and schedule a trailing timer for t=200.
At t=100 a timer already exists, so we only replace the saved args. The timer is not reset; that is how throttle differs from debounce.
At t=150 the same happens. The saved args are now [30], the most recent value.
At t=200 the trailing timer fires with the latest value, 30. Values 10 and 20 were skipped on purpose, but the final one was not lost.
At t=600 the window ended long ago, so remaining is negative and fn runs at once again.

followups.q: How can you build throttle out of debounce?
followups.a: A debounce with `leading: true` and `maxWait` equal to `wait` behaves like throttle. Lodash implements its throttle exactly this way.

followups.q: Why use performance.now() instead of Date.now()?
followups.a: `Date.now()` follows the wall clock, which NTP or a user can move backwards or forwards. `performance.now()` is monotonic, so measured intervals are always correct.

followups.q: Is throttle the same as rate limiting an API?
followups.a: No. Throttle drops or merges calls for one function in one process. API rate limiting counts requests per client key, often across many servers, and rejects with 429.

mistakes: Only implementing the leading edge, so the last update in a burst is lost.
Resetting the timer on every call, which turns throttle into debounce.
Using the first saved arguments on the trailing call instead of the latest.
Forgetting to clear the trailing timer when a leading call runs, which causes a double call.

questions.title: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter
questions.question: Write a retry helper for an async function with exponential backoff and jitter. Which errors should it retry?
questions.short: I loop: try the call, and on failure decide whether to retry. Only retry errors that are likely temporary, such as timeouts, connection resets, 429 and 5xx, and only for idempotent operations. The delay grows as base times 2 to the attempt, capped at a maximum, and I use full jitter: a random value between 0 and that number, so many clients do not retry at the same moment. After the last attempt I rethrow the original error. I also respect Retry-After and an AbortSignal.
questions.simple: If a shop is closed, you come back in 1 minute, then 2, then 4. And you add a random few seconds so the whole crowd does not come back at the exact same time.

explain.p: Write `retry(fn, options)` that calls an async function and, if it fails with a retryable error, tries again after a growing, randomized delay. Give up after `retries` extra attempts and throw the last error.

list: Loop with an attempt counter; `return await fn()` inside `try` so rejections are caught.
In `catch`, stop if attempts are used up or `shouldRetry(err)` says no (for example 400, 401, 404, validation errors).
Delay = `min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt)`, then apply full jitter: `random() * delay`. Jitter spreads retries out and prevents a "thundering herd".
If the server sent `Retry-After`, wait at least that long.
Accept an `AbortSignal` so a shutdown or a caller timeout can stop the retry loop, including the sleep.
Worst-case extra latency is the sum of delays, at most about `cap * retries`. Keep the total under the caller's own timeout.
Only retry idempotent operations (GET, PUT with the same body, or POST with an idempotency key). Retrying a non-idempotent payment can charge twice.
Retries multiply load. With 3 layers each doing 3 retries, one user request can become 27 calls to the database. Retry at one layer only.
Always rethrow the original error so callers see the real cause, or wrap it with `{ cause: err }`.
For long-lived failures pair retries with a circuit breaker so you stop hammering a dead dependency.

explain.note: What interviewers look for: a selective `shouldRetry` (not everything), a cap on the delay, jitter with a reason why, idempotency awareness, and cancellation. Saying "retry amplification across layers" is a strong senior signal.

anim.title: Two retries succeed, a 400 is not retried

steps.note: Attempt 0 calls flakyFetch. It throws 503 #1. Because we used return await inside try, the rejection lands in our catch.
The second retry call starts right away too. Its function rejects with 400.
Job A catch: 503 is retryable. Exponential part is 100 * 2^0 = 100ms. Full jitter picks random * 100; our fixed random 0.5 gives 50ms.
Job B catch: shouldRetry says a 400 will never succeed, so we rethrow at once instead of wasting time.
At t=50 job A wakes, tries again and fails with 503 #2. Delay doubles: 100 * 2^1 = 200, times 0.5 = 100ms.
At t=150 attempt 2 runs. The service is back, so fn returns data and retry resolves.
The caller only sees the success. Three calls total; the two failures were absorbed by the backoff.

followups.q: Why full jitter instead of a fixed exponential delay?
followups.a: If 1,000 clients fail at the same time, a fixed schedule makes them all retry at the same instants, causing new spikes. Full jitter spreads the retries evenly over the window, which AWS showed gives the lowest total load.

followups.q: Why `return await fn()` and not `return fn()` inside try?
followups.a: Without `await`, the promise is returned before it settles, so a later rejection skips the catch block entirely and no retry happens.

followups.q: How do you avoid retrying a request that already succeeded on the server?
followups.a: Make the operation idempotent: send an idempotency key that the server stores with the result, so a repeated request returns the stored result instead of doing the work again.

mistakes: Retrying every error, including 400/401/404 and programmer bugs.
No cap on the delay, so attempt 10 waits many minutes.
No jitter, so all clients retry in lockstep.
Using `return fn()` in try, so async failures are never caught.

questions.title: Implement promisify
questions.question: Write promisify(fn) that turns a Node-style callback function into one that returns a promise.
questions.short: promisify returns a new function. When called, it creates a promise and calls the original function with the same arguments plus one extra callback at the end. That callback follows the error-first convention: if err is set I reject, otherwise I resolve with the value. I use a regular function and fn.call(this, ...) so methods keep their this. Node's util.promisify also honors a custom symbol, util.promisify.custom, for functions that do not fit the pattern.
questions.simple: It is like replacing "call me back when you are done" with "give me a ticket I can check later". The ticket fills in when the callback fires.

explain.p: Node callback APIs look like `fn(arg1, arg2, (err, result) => {})`. Write `promisify(fn)` so you can write `const result = await promisify(fn)(arg1, arg2)` instead.

list: Return a wrapper `function (...args)`. A regular function, not an arrow, so `this` is forwarded.
Inside, return `new Promise((resolve, reject) => ...)` and call `fn.call(this, ...args, callback)`.
The callback: `if (err) reject(err); else resolve(value)`.
If `fn` throws synchronously, the promise executor catches it and rejects automatically.
If the callback is wrongly called twice, the second call is ignored, because a promise settles only once.
Bonus: check `fn[util.promisify.custom]` first, like Node does.
O(1) overhead per call: one promise and one closure.

Only the first success value is passed on. Callbacks with several results (like `(err, bytesRead, buffer)`) need a custom promisify or the built-in promise API (`fs.promises`, `dns.promises`, `timers/promises`).
Methods lose `this` if you promisify a detached function like `obj.method`. Bind it or call the wrapper as a method.

Do not promisify functions whose callback is not error-first (for example `setTimeout`). That is what `util.promisify.custom` is for: `util.promisify(setTimeout)` works because Node defines a custom version.
In real code prefer the built-in `util.promisify` or the promise-native APIs.

explain.note: What interviewers look for: error-first handling, forwarding `this` with a regular function, knowing sync throws inside the executor become rejections, and awareness of `util.promisify.custom` and the `fs/promises` style APIs.

anim.title: promisify turning callbacks into await

steps.note: promisify does no work yet. It just returns a wrapper that remembers fn in a closure.
main() starts and prints. Everything so far is synchronous.
The wrapper creates a promise and calls readConfig('app', cb), adding our callback as the last argument. readConfig sets a 50ms timer.
main hits await and pauses. The call stack is empty; the event loop waits for the timer.
At t=50 readConfig calls cb(null, value). err is null, so we resolve p1 with the config object.
main resumes after await with the value, as if the function had returned it.
A second call creates p2. readConfig schedules cb(err) for 50ms later, and main pauses again.
The callback gets an error as its first argument, so we reject p2 with it.
A rejected await throws at that line, so a normal try/catch handles the callback error.

followups.q: How do you go the other way, promise to callback?
followups.a: Use `util.callbackify(asyncFn)`. It calls the async function and invokes the callback with `(err)` on rejection or `(null, value)` on success. A falsy rejection reason is wrapped in an Error.

followups.q: Why does util.promisify(setTimeout) work even though setTimeout is not error-first?
followups.a: Node attaches a custom implementation under `util.promisify.custom`, and promisify returns that instead of wrapping. The same idea is exposed as `require("node:timers/promises").setTimeout`.

followups.q: What happens if the original function throws synchronously?
followups.a: The throw happens inside the Promise executor, which catches it and rejects the promise. The caller sees a rejection, not a sync exception.

mistakes: Using an arrow function wrapper and losing `this` for methods.
Putting the callback first instead of last.
Resolving with `err` or checking `if (value)` instead of `if (err)`.
Promisifying APIs that already have a promise version, such as `fs.promises.readFile`.

questions.title: LRU cache with O(1) get and set
questions.question: Implement an LRU cache with a fixed capacity where get and set are both O(1).
questions.short: In JavaScript a Map remembers insertion order, so I use that order as the recency order. On get, I delete the key and set it again, which moves it to the newest end. On set, I do the same, then if the size is over capacity I evict the oldest key, which is map.keys().next().value. Every operation is O(1). In other languages the classic answer is a hash map plus a doubly linked list, and that is exactly what Map gives us here.
questions.simple: It is a small bookshelf. Every book you read goes back on the right end. When the shelf is full, you remove the book on the far left, the one nobody touched for longest.

explain.p: Build `LRUCache(capacity)` with `get(key)` and `set(key, value)`. When the cache is full and a new key is added, remove the least recently used key. Both a successful `get` and a `set` count as "use".

list: `Map` keeps keys in insertion order, and delete plus set moves a key to the end. So the first key is always the least recently used.
`get`: if missing return `undefined`; else delete and re-insert, return value.
`set`: delete if present, insert, then while `size > capacity` delete the first key.
Use `has` to check presence, not the value, because a stored `undefined` or `0` is still a hit.
Without an ordered Map, use a hash map from key to node plus a doubly linked list with head and tail sentinels.
get, set, delete: O(1) average. Memory: O(capacity).
Updating an existing key must also refresh its position, not just its value.
Values that are `undefined` or falsy: check with `has`, not truthiness.
Objects as keys use reference identity. For composite keys build a string key.
Capacity by count is simple; production caches often limit by bytes or add a TTL. The `lru-cache` package supports both.
This is per-process memory. With several Node processes or pods, each has its own cache, so data can differ between them.

explain.note: If the interviewer says "no Map tricks", build the linked list: each node has prev/next, a map from key to node, `moveToFront(node)` and `removeTail()`. Sentinel head and tail nodes remove all the null checks.

What interviewers look for: O(1) for both operations and why, refreshing order on get, using the Map ordering correctly (`keys().next().value`), and the ability to explain the linked-list version on request.

anim.title: LRU with capacity 2

steps.note: Empty cache with room for two entries. The left end of the Map will always be the least recently used key.
a is new, so it is inserted at the end.
b goes after a. Size is 2, equal to capacity, so nothing is evicted.
get(a) deletes a and inserts it again, which moves it to the newest end. Now b is the oldest.
set(c) inserts c at the end. Size is now 3, which is over capacity.
The first key in the Map is the least recently used: b. Getting it from the iterator is O(1).
b is deleted. Note that a survived only because we read it a moment ago.
b is gone, so get returns undefined and the order does not change.
Final order from oldest to newest: a, then c.

followups.q: How would you add a TTL to each entry?
followups.a: Store `{ value, expires }`. In `get`, if `Date.now() > expires`, delete it and return a miss. Expired entries that are never read still use memory, so also evict expired ones during `set` or with a periodic sweep using an unref'd timer.

followups.q: Why not use a plain object instead of a Map?
followups.a: Object key order has special rules (integer-like keys are sorted first), keys are always strings, and there is no O(1) "first key" accessor. Map keeps true insertion order and allows any key type.

followups.q: When is LRU a bad policy?
followups.a: With scans: one big pass over many keys pushes out the whole hot set. LFU or segmented LRU handles that better.

mistakes: Forgetting to move a key to the newest end on `get`.
Using an array and `indexOf`/`splice`, which is O(n).
Checking `if (!value)` for misses, so cached `0` or `""` look like misses.
Not refreshing position when an existing key is updated with `set`.

questions.title: Token-bucket rate limiter middleware
questions.question: Write Express middleware that rate limits each client IP with a token bucket: a burst of up to N requests, refilling at R per second. Return 429 when the bucket is empty.
questions.short: Each IP gets a bucket with a capacity and a last-refill time, stored in a Map. On every request I refill lazily: add elapsed seconds times the rate, capped at capacity. If at least one token is left, I take it and call next(); otherwise I send 429 with a Retry-After header. There is no timer per bucket; I only do math when a request arrives. I clean up idle buckets so the Map does not grow forever, and in a multi-instance setup I would move the bucket into Redis with an atomic script.
questions.simple: Each visitor gets a jar of tickets. Every request costs one ticket, and the jar slowly refills by itself. An empty jar means "please wait".

explain.p: Write `rateLimit({ capacity, refillPerSec })` that returns `(req, res, next)` middleware. Each client (by `req.ip`) may burst up to `capacity` requests, then is limited to `refillPerSec` on average. Over the limit, respond `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After`.

list: Store `{ tokens, last }` per key in a Map. A new client starts full.
Lazy refill: `tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsedSec * refillPerSec)`. No `setInterval` per client.
If `tokens >= 1`, subtract 1 and call `next()`. Else compute how long until one token exists and send 429.
Add standard headers so clients can back off politely.
Remove buckets idle long enough to be full again; a fresh full bucket is the same thing.
Behind a proxy or load balancer set `app.set("trust proxy", ...)` correctly, or every request appears to come from the proxy IP.

explain.code:
# capacity 2, refill 1/sec, same IP
curl -i localhost:3000/api/x   # 200  RateLimit-Remaining: 1
curl -i localhost:3000/api/x   # 200  RateLimit-Remaining: 0
curl -i localhost:3000/api/x   # 429  Retry-After: 1
sleep 1
curl -i localhost:3000/api/x   # 200  RateLimit-Remaining: 0

list: O(1) per request. Memory is O(active clients); the sweeper keeps it bounded by recent traffic.
Per-process only: with 4 cluster workers or 10 pods each has its own Map, so the real limit is multiplied. Use Redis with a Lua script (read, refill, take, write atomically) for a shared limit.
Fractional tokens are fine and give a smooth rate; only `Retry-After` needs rounding up.
Wall-clock jumps can add or remove tokens. `performance.now()` avoids that inside one process.
IP is a weak key: many users can share one NAT IP. Prefer an API key or user id when the request is authenticated.
Put the limiter early in the chain, before expensive work like body parsing of large payloads or DB calls.

explain.note: What interviewers look for: lazy refill instead of timers, a capped bucket, correct 429 with Retry-After, memory cleanup for the Map, `trust proxy` awareness, and the multi-instance problem with a Redis answer.

anim.title: Token buckets for two IPs

steps.note: The limiter is created with capacity 2 and refill 1 token per second. We inject a fake clock so the demo is exact.
First request from 1.1.1.1: there is no bucket yet, so we create a full one with 2 tokens.
Refill adds nothing (0 seconds passed). We take one token and call next(), so the request goes through.
Second request at the same instant takes the last token. Bursts up to capacity are allowed.
Third request: 0 tokens. We need 1 more token at 1 per second, so Retry-After is 1 second, and we send 429 without calling next().
A different IP has its own bucket, so one noisy client does not block others.
At t=1000ms, 1.1.1.1 returns. One second passed, so lazy refill adds exactly 1 token, capped at capacity 2.
The refilled token is spent and the request is allowed. No timers were needed; all refill was computed on demand.

followups.q: Token bucket vs fixed window counter?
followups.a: A fixed window (100 requests per minute) allows a double burst at the window edge: 100 at 0:59 and 100 at 1:00. A token bucket gives a smooth average rate with a controlled burst size, and needs only two numbers per key.

followups.q: How do you make it work across several servers?
followups.a: Keep the bucket in Redis and do read, refill, take and write in one Lua script (or use a library built on it) so the check is atomic. Use Redis server time or pass the time in, and set a key TTL so idle buckets expire.

followups.q: What does req.ip return behind a load balancer?
followups.a: Without `trust proxy` it is the load balancer's address, so everyone shares one bucket. With `trust proxy` set to the right number of hops, Express reads the client address from `X-Forwarded-For`. Trusting too much lets clients spoof that header.

mistakes: Using a setInterval per client to add tokens, which wastes timers and memory.
Never deleting buckets, so the Map grows with every IP ever seen.
Forgetting `trust proxy`, so all traffic is limited as one client.
Assuming an in-memory limiter is global when the app runs in several processes.

questions.title: Count lines and words in a huge file
questions.question: You have a 20 GB log file. Count its lines and words in Node.js without loading it into memory.
questions.short: I read it with fs.createReadStream, which gives chunks of 64 KiB by default, so memory stays flat no matter how big the file is. I consume it with for await, which also handles backpressure. The tricky part is that a chunk can end in the middle of a line or word, so I carry state across chunks: either a leftover tail string, or, faster, I count newline bytes directly in the Buffer and track an "inside a word" flag. At the end I add one line if the file does not end with a newline. readline with crlfDelay: Infinity is the simple alternative.
questions.simple: It is like counting pages in a giant book by reading one handful of pages at a time and keeping a tally, instead of trying to hold the whole book at once.

explain.p: Write `countFile(path)` that returns `{ lines, words, bytes }` for a file of any size, with memory use that does not grow with the file.

list: `fs.readFile` would allocate the whole file. It also refuses files over 2 GiB (`ERR_FS_FILE_TOO_LARGE`), so a 20 GB file would fail outright.
Use `fs.createReadStream(path)` and `for await (const chunk of stream)`. The loop pulls one chunk at a time; reading pauses while you process it.
Chunk edges are random. "foo bar" might arrive as "fo" and "o bar". Keep state across chunks so you never split a line or word.
Fast way: work on raw bytes. The newline byte `0x0a` never appears inside a multi-byte UTF-8 character, so counting it in a Buffer is safe and avoids decoding to strings.
Simple way: `readline.createInterface({ input, crlfDelay: Infinity })` and `for await (const line of rl)`.
Last line: if the file does not end with a newline, that last line still counts.
Time O(file size); it is I/O bound. Memory O(chunk size), about 64 KiB plus overhead.

Windows line endings `
`: byte counting still works because it counts `
`; readline needs `crlfDelay: Infinity` to treat `
` as one break.
Multi-byte characters split across chunks: decoding each chunk with `chunk.toString()` corrupts them. Use the byte approach, `setEncoding("utf8")` (which uses a StringDecoder), or readline.
Very long lines (no newline for gigabytes) make the readline approach buffer that whole line. The byte approach does not care.
Empty file: 0 lines. A file with just "\n": 1 line.
Speed tips: a bigger `highWaterMark` (like 1 MiB) reduces syscalls for big sequential reads.

explain.note: What interviewers look for: streaming instead of `readFile`, `for await` (backpressure for free), correct handling of chunk boundaries and the final line without newline, and awareness of UTF-8 splitting. Mentioning the byte-level `0x0a` trick is a strong signal.

anim.title: Counting across 16-byte chunks

steps.note: The demo writes a small 45-byte file. Its last line has no trailing newline on purpose.
createReadStream opens the file but reads lazily. highWaterMark 16 makes chunks tiny so we can watch the boundaries; real code uses the 64 KiB default.
Chunk 1 is "hello world\nfoo ". Splitting on newline gives one complete line and a piece that may continue.
The last piece "foo " is kept as the tail, because the rest of that line is in the next chunk. One full line counted: 2 words.
Chunk 2 is joined to the tail: "foo bar baz\n\nlast li". That yields "foo bar baz" and an empty line. "last li" is the new tail.
Chunk 3 has no newline at all, so the whole joined text becomes the tail and no line is counted yet.
The 'end' event fires. The tail is not empty, so it is the final line without a newline. Forgetting this step is the classic off-by-one.
Results: 4 lines, 9 words, 45 bytes. Memory never held more than one chunk plus one partial line.

followups.q: Why not fs.readFile and split?
followups.a: It loads the whole file into memory, then makes a second copy as a string and a third as an array of lines. For large files that is slow, may hit the max Buffer or string length, and can crash the process with out-of-memory.

followups.q: How would you make it faster on a multi-core machine?
followups.a: Split the file into byte ranges, read each with `createReadStream(path, { start, end })` in `worker_threads`, and fix up words split at range edges. Usually the disk, not the CPU, is the limit.

followups.q: What is backpressure here?
followups.a: If processing is slower than reading, the stream must stop reading. `for await` does that automatically: the stream is paused until the loop body finishes. With the `data` event you would need `pause()`/`resume()` for async work.

mistakes: Using `fs.readFile` for a file that can be bigger than memory.
Counting lines per chunk and ignoring that chunks split lines and words.
Calling `chunk.toString()` per chunk, which breaks multi-byte UTF-8 characters at boundaries.
Missing the last line when the file does not end with a newline.

questions.title: TTL cache and async memoize
questions.question: Build an in-memory cache with a TTL, and use it to memoize an async function so that 100 concurrent calls with the same key hit the database only once.
questions.short: The cache stores { value, expires } per key and treats expired entries as misses, deleting them lazily on read plus with a periodic sweep. For memoizing async functions the key idea is to cache the promise, not the result. The first caller stores the in-flight promise right away, so every concurrent caller gets the same promise and the database is hit once. If the promise rejects, I remove it so errors are not cached. I also cap the size so the cache cannot grow without limit.
questions.simple: If ten people ask you the same question while you are still looking it up, you do not look it up ten times. You tell them all "wait, I am checking", and give everyone the same answer, which you then remember for a while.

explain.p: Part 1: `TTLCache` with `get`, `set`, `delete`, where entries vanish after `ttlMs`. Part 2: `memoizeAsync(fn, options)` that caches results of an async function, de-duplicates concurrent calls for the same key, and never caches failures.

list: Expiry: store `expires = Date.now() + ttl`. On `get`, if expired, delete and return a miss (lazy expiry).
Lazy expiry alone leaks keys that are never read again, so add a sweep on an unref'd interval and a max size.
Memoize: put the promise in the cache before awaiting it. Concurrent callers find the pending promise and share it. This prevents a "cache stampede".
On rejection, delete the entry (only if it is still ours), so the next call retries.
Start the TTL when the value arrives, not when the request started, or a slow call can expire the moment it finishes.
get/set: O(1). Sweep: O(n) but rare and in the background.
Values are wrapped (`{ value }`) so a cached `undefined` result is still a hit.
Keys: `JSON.stringify(args)` is simple but object key order matters and it fails on BigInt or cycles. Pass a custom `key` function for real code.
Cached objects are shared by reference. If a caller mutates one, every later caller sees it. Freeze or clone if that matters.
Per-process: each instance has its own cache and invalidation is local. For shared data use Redis, and invalidate on writes.
Unbounded caches are a common Node memory leak. Always cap by size and TTL.

explain.note: What interviewers look for: caching the promise to de-duplicate in-flight calls, not caching rejections, bounded memory (TTL plus max size plus sweep with `unref`), and awareness of stale reads and per-instance caches.

anim.title: Two concurrent calls, one DB query, then expiry

steps.note: main calls getUser(1) twice inside Promise.all. The first call misses the cache, so the real function starts and logs the query.
Before awaiting anything, the pending promise is stored under key 1. This is the trick that de-duplicates concurrent calls.
The second getUser(1) runs immediately after. It finds the pending promise and returns the same one. No second DB query.
At t=50 the query finishes. Both callers get the very same object from the one promise.
A third call within 200ms gets the settled promise from the cache. Awaiting it is instant; dbCalls stays at 1.
We wait 250ms. The entry passes its expiry time, but nothing deletes it yet; expiry is checked lazily on the next read.
getUser(1) reads the entry, sees it is expired, deletes it and reports a miss.
A miss means a fresh query and a fresh promise stored in the cache.
Two DB calls in total for four getUser calls. In this short version the TTL starts when the request starts; the full version starts it when data arrives.

followups.q: What is a cache stampede and how does this help?
followups.a: When a popular key expires, many requests miss at once and all hit the database together. Sharing the in-flight promise collapses them into one query per process. Across many instances you also need jittered TTLs or a distributed lock.

followups.q: What is stale-while-revalidate?
followups.a: After the TTL, keep serving the old value immediately while one background refresh fetches a new one. Users never wait on the refresh, at the cost of briefly stale data.

followups.q: Why should rejections not be cached?
followups.a: Errors are usually temporary (a timeout, a restart). Caching a rejected promise would make every caller fail for the whole TTL even after the database recovers.

mistakes: Caching the result after `await`, so concurrent callers all miss and all query the database.
Caching rejected promises, which turns a brief outage into a long one.
No max size and no sweep, causing a slow memory leak in a long-running process.
Using `if (cached)` so falsy results like `0` or `null` are never cache hits.

questions.title: withTimeout using AbortController
questions.question: Write withTimeout(task, ms) that rejects if the task takes too long, and actually cancels the underlying work, not just stops waiting for it.
questions.short: I race the task against a timer promise with Promise.race. But race alone only stops waiting; the work keeps running. So I create an AbortController, pass its signal into the task, and when the timer fires I call controller.abort(err) before rejecting. Tasks like fetch or my own code listen to the signal and stop. In finally I clear the timer so a fast task does not leave a timer keeping the process alive. For simple cases AbortSignal.timeout(ms) does the same thing in one line.
questions.simple: It is like ordering food with a deadline: if it is not ready in 20 minutes you leave, and you also phone the kitchen to stop cooking, instead of letting them finish a meal nobody will eat.

explain.p: Write `withTimeout(task, ms)` where `task` is `(signal) => Promise`. Resolve with the task result if it finishes in time. Otherwise reject with a `TimeoutError` and abort the signal so the task stops its work.

list: Create an `AbortController` and pass `controller.signal` to the task.
Create a timeout promise whose timer calls `controller.abort(err)` and then `reject(err)`.
`Promise.race([taskPromise, timeoutPromise])` settles with whichever finishes first.
`.finally(() => clearTimeout(timer))` removes the timer when the task wins.
Let a caller pass its own signal too, and combine both with `AbortSignal.any([parent, controller.signal])` (Node 20.3+).
Tasks must cooperate: pass the signal to `fetch`, `timers/promises`, `stream.pipeline`, or listen for `"abort"` yourself.
O(1) overhead: one timer, one controller, two promises.
Without `clearTimeout`, every fast call leaves a live timer that holds memory and keeps the process from exiting until it fires.
Promise.race does not cancel anything by itself. Without the signal, a timed-out DB query or HTTP call keeps running and using a connection.
Tasks that ignore the signal still run to completion; withTimeout can only stop waiting. Document that tasks must honor `signal`.
The losing promise may still reject later. `Promise.race` already attached handlers to it, so there is no unhandled rejection warning.
Check `signal.aborted` before starting expensive steps, or call `signal.throwIfAborted()`.

explain.note: What interviewers look for: knowing that `Promise.race` alone leaks work, wiring an AbortSignal into the task, clearing the timer in `finally`, a distinct `TimeoutError`, and knowing the built-ins `AbortSignal.timeout` and `AbortSignal.any`.

anim.title: A fast task wins; a slow task is aborted

steps.note: First call: a 50ms job with a 200ms limit. withTimeout creates a controller and a timeout timer.
The task gets the signal. slowJob schedules its own 50ms timer and subscribes to the abort event.
Promise.race waits for whichever settles first: the job or the timeout.
At t=50 the job wins. finally clears the 200ms timer, so no stray timer is left behind.
Second call: a 500ms job with only a 100ms limit. Both timers are now pending.
At +100ms the timeout fires first. It builds a TimeoutError and aborts the controller with it as the reason.
abort() runs the listener synchronously: the job clears its 500ms timer and rejects. The real work stopped, not just our waiting.
The race rejects with the TimeoutError and main catches it. No timers remain, so the process exits right away instead of at 500ms.

followups.q: What is AbortSignal.timeout(ms)?
followups.a: A static method that returns a signal which aborts by itself after `ms` with a `TimeoutError` DOMException. It is the simplest option when the API already takes a signal, like `fetch` or `timers/promises`.

followups.q: How do you combine a user cancel signal with a timeout?
followups.a: Use `AbortSignal.any([userSignal, AbortSignal.timeout(ms)])`. The combined signal aborts when either source aborts, and its `reason` tells you which one.

followups.q: How would you cancel a database query on timeout?
followups.a: Pass the signal into the driver if it supports one, or on abort call the driver's cancel method (for Postgres, a cancel request for that backend). Also set a server-side statement timeout as a safety net.

mistakes: Using only Promise.race and thinking the slow operation was cancelled.
Not clearing the timer when the task wins, leaking timers and delaying process exit.
Creating the AbortController but never passing its signal into the actual work.
Throwing a generic Error so callers cannot tell a timeout from other failures.
